claims.claim: The transcriptional profiles of projection neurons develop independently of motor partner-derived signals.
claims.source: Nevertheless, consistent with functional and anatomical characterization, our sequencing data argues that projection neurons acquire the correct transcriptional profiles in the absence of motor partner-derived signals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the minimal differential gene expression observed.

claims.claim: The current model for vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit development must be revised: up/down projection neuron subtype fate cannot be retrogradely established by a motor partner-derived signal.
claims.source: The current model of vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit development must therefore be revised: up/down projection neuron subtype fate cannot be retrogradely established by a motor partner-derived signal.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective findings that contradict the retrograde model.

claims.claim: The signals that specify projection neuron fate must lie elsewhere, not from motor partners.
claims.source: Instead, the signals that specify fate must lie elsewhere.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that motor neurons are dispensable for fate specification.

claims.claim: phox2a acts in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner to specify extraocular motor pool fate.
claims.source: While the primary focus of our work was circuit assembly, we found that, unexpectedly, phox2a acts in a dose-dependent manner to specify extraocular motor pool fate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that heterozygotes lose specific early-born neurons.

claims.claim: In phox2a heterozygotes, the earliest-born dorsal neurons in nIII are lost but later-born neurons in nIII/nIV are intact.
claims.source: Key evidence comes from phox2a heterozygotes, in which the earliest-born dorsal neurons in nIII are lost but later-born neurons in nIII/nIV are intact.
claims.evidence: This is data from cell counting and spatial mapping experiments.

claims.claim: Partial phox2a dosage preferentially targets the earliest-born neurons.
claims.source: Specifically, if phox2a is expressed in neural progenitor cells that give rise to nIII/nIV, then the earliest-born motor neurons would have the shortest exposure to phox2a.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the dose-dependent effect.

claims.claim: Extraocular motor neuron axons do not serve as 'pioneers' for pre-motor axon targeting.
claims.source: We find that extraocular motor neuron axons do not serve as 'pioneers' (Supèr et al., 1998, McConnell et al., 1989, Bentley and Keshishian, 1982, Bate, 1976, Pike et al., 1992), with pre-motor axon targeting following passively from motor-derived pathfinding signals (Matise and Lance-Jones, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that projection neurons still establish appropriate projections in the absence of motor neurons.

claims.claim: Projection neurons still establish long-range (hindbrain to midbrain) axonal projections with appropriate spatial segregation in the absence of motor neurons.
claims.source: Instead, we observed that projection neurons still establish long-range (hindbrain to midbrain) axonal projections, with appropriate spatial segregation that matches the topography of their motor partners (Greaney et al., 2017, Liu et al., 2022, Goldblatt et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is data from anatomical imaging experiments.

claims.claim: The proper spatial and temporal segregation of projection neuron axons suggests they remain poised to wire with spatially-appropriate targets.
claims.source: Here, the proper spatial and temporal segregation of projection neuron axons suggests they remain poised to wire with spatially-appropriate (dorsal/ventral pools) targets.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical imaging data.

claims.claim: Projection neuron axons do not require a target-derived cue to grow, search, and synapse onto motor targets, and simply lack the adhesive contact necessary to stabilize nascent structures.
claims.source: We predict that projection neuron axons do not require a target-derived cue to grow, search, and synapse onto motor targets, and simply lack the adhesive contact necessary to stabilize nascent structures (reviewed in Dalva et al., 2007; Moreland and Poulain, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the anatomical findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Extraocular motor neurons might still play an active or passive role in selecting and/or refining input specificity from their projection neuron partners.
claims.source: Nevertheless, extraocular motor neurons might still play an active or passive role in selecting and/or refining input specificity from their projection neuron partners.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential roles not tested in this study.

claims.claim: Projection neurons also contact neurons in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC/nMLF).
claims.source: We note that our study does not eliminate one additional source of post-synaptic partner signals to projection neurons. As in primates (McCrea et al., 1987), projection neurons also contact neurons in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal, also known as the nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (INC/nMLF; Bianco et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about circuit connectivity, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Projection neuron connectivity to INC/nMLF targets is present and functional in phox2a mutants.
claims.source: As we did not observe postural deficits in phox2a mutants, we infer that projection neuron connectivity to INC/nMLF targets is present and functional.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of postural deficits.

claims.claim: The development of projection neuron collaterals and synapses to INC/nMLF neurons appeared qualitatively normal in phox2a mutants.
claims.source: Correspondingly, the development of projection neuron collaterals and synapses to INC/nMLF neurons appeared qualitatively normal in phox2a mutants, supporting our interpretation that projection neurons retain the capacity to properly assemble with post-synaptic targets even though similar structures to extraocular motor neurons are absent.
claims.evidence: This is anatomical imaging data.

claims.claim: The tight links between birth order, somatic position, and stimulus selectivity across vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit populations support an 'intrinsic' determination model.
claims.source: The tight links between birth order, somatic position, and stimulus selectivity (Greaney et al., 2017, Goldblatt et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2022, Tanimoto et al., 2022, Zecca et al., 2015, Dyballa et al., 2017) across vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit populations support an 'intrinsic' determination model.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from established patterns in the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neurogenesis and initial axon targeting develops contemporaneously for sensory afferents, projection neurons, and extraocular motor neurons.
claims.source: Further, neurogenesis and initial axon targeting develops contemporaneously for sensory afferents (Fritzsch and Nichols, 1993, Altman and Bayer, 1982, Vemaraju et al., 2012, Zecca et al., 2015), projection neurons (McConnell and Sechrist, 1980, Maklad and Fritzsch, 2003, Auclair et al., 1999, Glover, 2003, Goldblatt et al., 2023), and extraocular motor neurons (Greaney et al., 2017, Altman and Bayer, 1981, Glover, 2003, Shaw and Alley, 1981, Puelles and Privat, 1977, Varela-Echavarría et al., 1996), suggesting that neurons are poised to assemble with targets as early as their time of differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: An 'intrinsic specification' model predicts that projection neurons and extraocular motor neurons should be directionally selective as soon as pre-synaptic input is established.
claims.source: Importantly, an 'intrinsic specification' model makes a testable prediction about how and when sensory selectivity should emerge across the circuit: projection neurons and extraocular motor neurons should be directionally selective as soon as pre-synaptic input is established.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the intrinsic model.

claims.claim: Evidence that stimulus selectivity emerges gradually would suggest that sensory afferents and/or projection neurons initially wire indiscriminately and that circuit connectivity is refined in time by extrinsic forces.
claims.source: Conversely, evidence that stimulus selectivity emerges gradually would suggest that sensory afferents and/or projection neurons initially wire indiscriminately and that circuit connectivity is refined in time by extrinsic forces.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

claims.claim: An 'extrinsic' determination model would predict that connectivity is established by an anterogradely-transmitted signal from sensory afferents to ocular muscles.
claims.source: Here, an 'extrinsic' determination model would predict that connectivity is established by an anterogradely-transmitted signal – that is, from sensory afferents to ocular muscles.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

results.result: The phox2a gene is a highly conserved transcription factor that specifies nIII/nIV motor neuron fate in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner. CRISPR/Cas9-generated phox2a mutants exhibit near-total loss of nIII/nIV motor neurons, exotropic eyes, failure to hatch, and lethality by 7 dpf. Heterozygotes show selective loss of early-born dorsal nIII neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C17 collectively establish phox2a as a critical transcription factor for motor neuron specification. The genetic characterization is thorough, with quantitative cell counts (C13: p=2.5×10⁻⁴), molecular validation via vachta expression (C14), and dose-dependent effects in heterozygotes (C15-C16). The phenotypic observations (C10-C12) are consistent with prior literature and provide clear validation of the loss-of-function model.

results.result: Projection neurons in phox2a mutants show normal functional responses to tonic tilt stimuli, with preserved directional selectivity, response magnitudes, and topographic organization. The number and ratio of projection neuron subtypes are unchanged, and only a minor spatial shift (2 µm) within registration error is observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C27 provide comprehensive functional and spatial characterization using calcium imaging (n=297 neurons from 16 mutants vs. 440 from 21 controls). Statistical analyses show no significant differences in response magnitudes (C25: p=0.98, p=0.18) or directional selectivity (C26: p=0.85, p=0.12). The minor spatial shift (C22-C23) is appropriately contextualized as within experimental error. This strongly supports that sensory-to-projection neuron connectivity develops independently of motor partners.

results.result: Projection neurons in phox2a mutants respond normally to impulse tilt stimuli from semicircular canals, with comparable response ratios, magnitudes, spatial localization, and lack of directional selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 extend the functional analysis to phasic sensory inputs. The data show preserved impulse responses (C28: 58% vs. 71% responsive), unchanged response magnitudes (C30: p=0.85), and maintained spatial localization (C29: p=0.99). This complements the tonic tilt data and strengthens the conclusion that motor partners are dispensable for sensory-to-projection neuron connectivity.

results.result: Projection neurons in phox2a mutants successfully initiate axon outgrowth and maintain appropriate dorsoventral spatial segregation at midbrain targets. While collaterals to nIII/nIV are absent, projection neurons retain the capacity to form collaterals when residual motor neurons are present and robustly arborize to other targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 use retrograde photolabeling and anatomical imaging to demonstrate that projection neurons establish long-range projections with appropriate topography despite motor neuron loss. The observation that occasional collaterals form when 1-5% of motor neurons remain (C37) and that arborization to other targets is intact (C36) supports the interpretation that projection neurons are competent to assemble but lack stabilizing contacts (C38). This is consistent with the authors' model.

results.result: Projection neurons in phox2a mutants express pre-synaptic markers (synaptophysin a, synaptic vesicle glycoprotein, synapsin I) at normal levels, indicating they develop the molecular machinery for synaptogenesis independently of motor partners. The absence of collaterals and synapses likely reflects lack of adhesive stabilization rather than instructive signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 use fluorescent in situ hybridization to show preserved expression of pre-synaptic markers in phox2a mutants. The data support that projection neurons are molecularly poised for synaptogenesis (C40-C41). However, C42 is speculative and relies on citations rather than direct experimental evidence. The overall conclusion that motor neurons are not required for molecular development is well-supported, though the mechanistic interpretation (adhesion vs. instruction) remains inferential.

results.result: Bulk RNA sequencing reveals strikingly few differentially expressed genes in projection neurons between phox2a mutants and controls. All candidate genes are lowly expressed (<10% detection in reference neurons), and fluorescent in situ validation shows no differences in expression patterns. The transcriptional profiles of projection neurons develop independently of motor partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 use bulk RNA-seq with single-cell reference filtering to assess transcriptional changes. The minimal differential expression (C43-C44), lack of validation by in situ (C45), and high detection of top-expressed genes in reference data (C46) support the conclusion. The authors appropriately acknowledge potential limitations (contamination, insufficient sensitivity) but the convergent evidence from multiple approaches (bulk, single-cell, in situ) strengthens the conclusion that transcriptional profiles are motor-independent (C48).

results.result: Motor neurons are dispensable for proper connectivity in the vestibular reflex circuit. Projection neurons show normal functional responses, anatomical organization, molecular profiles, and transcriptional signatures in the absence of motor partners. This overturns the retrograde model that motor-derived signals specify projection neuron fate and connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C49-C50 represent the overarching conclusions synthesized from the functional (C2), anatomical (C3), and molecular (C4) data. The collective evidence from calcium imaging, retrograde labeling, in situ hybridization, and RNA-seq strongly supports that motor neurons are dispensable for projection neuron development. The claim that this overturns the retrograde model (C5, C49) is justified by the comprehensive negative results across multiple experimental modalities. However, the authors appropriately note that motor neurons may still play roles in refinement or selection (C58, C41).

results.result: phox2a acts in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner to specify extraocular motor pool fate. Heterozygotes selectively lose early-born dorsal nIII neurons while later-born neurons remain intact, suggesting that partial phox2a dosage preferentially affects neurons with shorter exposure during progenitor stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by quantitative cell counting and spatial mapping showing selective loss of early-born neurons in heterozygotes (C15-C16). However, C53 is speculative and lacks direct experimental evidence (e.g., lineage tracing, temporal expression analysis). The dose-dependent effect is well-documented, but the mechanistic explanation remains hypothetical.

results.result: Extraocular motor neuron axons do not serve as pioneers for pre-motor axon targeting. Projection neurons establish long-range projections with appropriate spatial segregation in the absence of motor neurons, suggesting they do not require target-derived cues but lack adhesive contacts for stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 synthesize anatomical findings (C34-C37) to argue against a pioneer axon model. The data showing preserved axon segregation (C55) and the ability to form collaterals when targets are present (C37) support this interpretation. However, C57 is speculative and relies on citations rather than direct experimental manipulation of adhesion molecules or stabilization factors.

results.result: Projection neurons also contact neurons in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC/nMLF). In phox2a mutants, projection neuron connectivity to INC/nMLF targets appears qualitatively normal, and the absence of postural deficits suggests this connectivity is functional.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is established knowledge supported by citations. However, C60 is an inference from the absence of postural deficits, which is not directly measured or quantified. C61 relies on qualitative anatomical observations without quantitative analysis. While plausible, the evidence is insufficient to definitively conclude that INC/nMLF connectivity is normal and functional in phox2a mutants.

results.result: The tight links between birth order, somatic position, and stimulus selectivity across vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit populations support an 'intrinsic' determination model. Neurogenesis and axon targeting develop contemporaneously, suggesting neurons are poised to assemble with targets early. This model predicts that directional selectivity should emerge as soon as pre-synaptic input is established.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are largely speculative and represent future directions rather than tested hypotheses. C62-C63 synthesize literature to propose an intrinsic model, but C64-C66 are untested predictions. While the authors appropriately frame these as testable hypotheses, they do not constitute supported results from the current study.

results.result: Extraocular motor neurons might still play an active or passive role in selecting and/or refining input specificity from their projection neuron partners.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is a speculative statement acknowledging potential roles not tested in this study. It appropriately qualifies the main conclusions but does not constitute a supported result.

results.result: The vertebrate vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit consists of three neuron types (peripheral sensory, central projection, and extraocular motor neurons) with directionally-tuned connectivity that stabilizes gaze after head/body tilts.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 describe established knowledge about circuit architecture, supported by multiple citations. This provides essential background context for the study but does not represent a novel finding.

results.result: The phox2a null mutant successfully ablates extraocular motor neurons (nIII/nIV), as evidenced by near-total loss of isl1 expression (WT: 298±19 neurons; null: 19±11 neurons; p=2.5×10⁻⁴), loss of vachta expression, exotropic eyes, and failure to hatch or inflate swim bladders, with lethality by 7 dpf.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the successful ablation of motor neurons. Reviewer 1 states the study 'shows that phox2a knockout ablates these motor neurons' and Reviewer 2 confirms 'the loss of function paradigm to eliminate extraocular motor neurons' was successful. The editor notes 'compelling and comprehensive genetic, anatomical and behavioral evidence.'

results.result: Projection neurons show normal functional responses to vestibular tilt stimuli in phox2a mutants, with comparable neuron numbers (control: 42±4; mutant: 39±3; p=0.22), subtype ratios (46-47% nose-down/up in controls vs. 49-44% in mutants), response magnitudes, directional selectivity, and spatial topography, indicating that functional connectivity between sensory neurons and projection neurons develops independently of motor partners.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously support these findings. Reviewer 1 states projection neurons have 'largely normal responses to vestibular input' and Reviewer 2 confirms 'the loss of function paradigm...did not alter the normal functional connections between peripheral sensory neurons and central projection neurons.' The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling and comprehensive.'

results.result: Projection neurons respond normally to impulse (phasic) vestibular stimuli in phox2a mutants, with comparable response ratios (58% vs. 71%), magnitudes (ΔF/F: 0.33±0.29 vs. 0.36±0.40; p=0.85), lack of directional selectivity, and ventral localization, demonstrating that connectivity with phasic sensory afferents does not require motor partners.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive functional characterization. Reviewer 2 notes the study demonstrates 'normal functional connections between peripheral sensory neurons and central projection neurons,' which encompasses both tonic and phasic responses. No concerns were raised about the impulse response data.

results.result: Projection neuron axons show normal initial outgrowth and dorsoventral segregation at midbrain targets in phox2a mutants, though they fail to form collaterals to absent nIII/nIV targets while maintaining robust arborization to other targets (nucleus of medial longitudinal fasciculus), indicating projection neurons remain anatomically competent to assemble with spatially-appropriate targets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the anatomical findings. Reviewer 1 states projection neurons have 'normal gross morphology' and Reviewer 2 confirms the study shows projection neurons 'affect the position of central projection neurons in the sensorimotor circuit' was not altered. The editor describes the anatomical evidence as 'compelling and comprehensive.'

results.result: Projection neurons express pre-synaptic markers (synaptophysin a, synaptic vesicle glycoprotein, synapsin I) normally in phox2a mutants at 5 dpf, indicating they remain molecularly poised to form synapses with appropriate targets, with absent collaterals likely reflecting lack of adhesive contact for stabilization rather than instructive signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the molecular characterization. Reviewer 1 notes projection neurons have 'minimally changed transcriptional profiles' and Reviewer 2 confirms the study demonstrates projection neurons do not 'significantly alter the transcriptional profiles.' The interpretation about adhesive contact is presented as speculation (C42) but reviewers do not challenge it.

results.result: Bulk RNA sequencing reveals strikingly few differentially-expressed genes between phox2a mutants and controls, with all candidate genes lowly-expressed (<10% detection in reference projection neurons) and showing no differences by in situ hybridization, indicating projection neuron transcriptional profiles develop independently of motor partner-derived signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the transcriptional findings. Reviewer 1 states projection neurons have 'minimally changed transcriptional profiles' and Reviewer 2 confirms 'the loss of function paradigm...did not significantly alter the transcriptional profiles of central projection neurons.' The comprehensive nature of the sequencing analysis is praised.

results.result: The collective findings overturn the retrograde model of circuit assembly, demonstrating that motor neurons are dispensable for proper connectivity in the vestibulo-ocular reflex circuit and that projection neuron subtype fate is not retrogradely established by motor partner-derived signals, requiring revision of the current developmental model.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this major conclusion. The editor states the study provides evidence 'that the answer is, "No!"' to whether motor neurons are required. Reviewer 1 concludes 'the wiring of the circuit is not instructed by the output neurons, refuting the major model.' Reviewer 2 states results 'strongly indicate that retrograde signals from motor neurons are not required.' Reviewer 3 presents 'a convincing argument for the dispensability of motor neurons.'

results.result: phox2a heterozygotes show reduced neuron numbers (229±20 vs. 298±19; p=6.7×10⁻⁴) with loss restricted to earliest-born medial dorsal nIII neurons, indicating phox2a acts in a dose- and birthdate-dependent manner to specify extraocular motor pool fate.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the heterozygote findings. While not extensively discussed in reviews, the data is presented as part of the comprehensive characterization of the phox2a mutant phenotype, and no reviewer questions the dose-dependent interpretation.

results.result: Extraocular motor neuron axons do not serve as 'pioneers' for pre-motor axon targeting; instead, projection neurons establish long-range axonal projections with appropriate spatial segregation independently, suggesting they do not require target-derived cues but simply lack adhesive contact to stabilize nascent structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation as part of the overall conclusion about motor neuron dispensability. Reviewer 1 notes 'the findings are interesting and should leave little doubt about the paper's main conclusions,' which encompasses the pioneer axon interpretation. The speculative component (C57) is not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: Projection neurons also contact neurons in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC/nMLF), and this connectivity appears qualitatively normal in phox2a mutants based on absence of postural deficits and normal collateral/synapse development to these targets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the INC/nMLF findings. Reviewer 1 notes as a future direction that 'the projection neurons innervate several other cell types that could affect their development,' acknowledging the presence of other postsynaptic partners without challenging the authors' interpretation of their normal development.

results.result: The authors propose an 'intrinsic determination' model based on tight links between birth order, position, and selectivity, and contemporaneous neurogenesis across circuit populations, predicting directional selectivity should emerge immediately upon pre-synaptic input establishment, contrasting with 'extrinsic' models involving gradual refinement or anterograde signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express concern about generalizability of the proposed model. Reviewer 2 states 'a concern is that the results presented may be limited to this specific circuit and may not be generalizable to other circuit assemblies' and notes 'whether generalizable to other circuits is debatable.' Reviewer 3 notes 'their claims about the generalizability of their findings to other sensorimotor circuits should be tempered.' The model itself is speculative (C64-C66) and reviewers indicate uncertainty about its broader applicability.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that extraocular motor neurons might still play active or passive roles in selecting and/or refining input specificity from projection neuron partners, representing potential later-stage functions not tested in this study.
results.evaluation: Reviewers appreciate this caveat. Reviewer 1 notes 'motor neurons may play later roles in selecting and/or refining pre-motor input specificity' as an appropriate limitation, and suggests future work could 'determine the precise contribution of each postsynaptic population on the projection neurons' development.' This acknowledgment is viewed positively as balanced interpretation.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the successful ablation of motor neurons via phox2a knockout (C8-C14). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative validation including cell counts and statistical significance (p=2.5×10⁻⁴), while peer reviewers affirm the genetic paradigm was successful with 'compelling and comprehensive' evidence. Both rate as SUPPORTED with strong agreement.

Both evaluations strongly support the functional characterization showing preserved sensory-to-projection neuron connectivity (C18-C27). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative calcium imaging data (n=297 vs 440 neurons) with specific p-values, while peer reviewers confirm 'largely normal responses' and 'normal functional connections.' Both conclude SUPPORTED with complete agreement that motor neurons are dispensable for this connectivity.

Perfect agreement on phasic sensory input findings (C28-C31). OpenEval details preserved impulse responses (58% vs 71%) with statistical validation (p=0.85, p=0.99), while peer reviewers accept these as part of comprehensive functional characterization without raising concerns. Both rate SUPPORTED.

Complete concordance on anatomical findings (C32-C38). OpenEval describes retrograde photolabeling showing appropriate topography and occasional collaterals when residual motor neurons remain, while peer reviewers confirm 'normal gross morphology' and 'compelling anatomical evidence.' Both rate SUPPORTED.

Both support molecular characterization via in situ hybridization (C39-C42). OpenEval notes preserved pre-synaptic marker expression but flags C42 as speculative regarding adhesion mechanisms. Peer reviewers accept the molecular findings and note the speculation is not challenged. Both rate SUPPORTED despite acknowledging inferential components.

Strong agreement on transcriptional profiling (C43-C48). OpenEval details bulk RNA-seq methodology with single-cell reference filtering and acknowledges potential limitations while concluding motor-independent transcription. Peer reviewers explicitly support 'minimally changed transcriptional profiles' and praise comprehensive sequencing. Both rate SUPPORTED.

Complete agreement on the major conclusion that motor neurons are dispensable for projection neuron development (C1, C5, C49-C50). OpenEval synthesizes evidence across multiple modalities, while peer reviewers unanimously affirm this conclusion with statements like 'convincing argument for dispensability' and 'refuting the major model.' Both rate SUPPORTED.

Both support heterozygote dose-dependent findings (C15-C16, C51-C53). OpenEval provides quantitative validation but notes C53 is speculative regarding mechanisms. Peer reviewers do not extensively discuss but accept as part of comprehensive characterization without raising concerns. Both rate SUPPORTED despite mechanistic speculation.

Agreement on rejecting pioneer axon model (C54-C57). OpenEval notes preserved axon segregation and ability to form collaterals when targets present, but flags C57 as speculative. Peer reviewers accept interpretation as part of overall dispensability conclusion without challenge. Both rate SUPPORTED.

Divergent evaluations of INC/nMLF connectivity claims (C59-C61). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to lack of quantitative measurement and reliance on qualitative observations. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED and do not raise concerns, acknowledging other postsynaptic partners without challenging the interpretation. This represents a notable disagreement in evidential standards.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding generalizability (C62-C66). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN noting these are speculative future directions rather than tested hypotheses. Peer reviewers also express UNCERTAIN, specifically concerned about generalizability to other circuits and recommend tempering claims. Both recognize these as untested predictions.

Divergent evaluations of caveat statement (C58). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN as speculative acknowledgment of untested roles. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, viewing this caveat positively as balanced interpretation and appropriate limitation. The difference reflects whether caveats qualify as 'supported' findings versus speculative statements.

OpenEval evaluated background claims about circuit architecture (C6-C7) as SUPPORTED established knowledge from citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not separately assess background context claims.
